Formed through runaway stellar collisions, nuclear star clusters (NSCs) located in the cores of many galaxies are believed to be densely populated with massive objects, including black holes (BHs), neutron stars (NSs), and "stalled" stars—runaway objects whose cores have ended their lives, but which retain degenerate surfaces. When these surface layers collapse, first-generation stellar populations (Pop III) will generate gravitational waves (GWs) detectable by third-generation detectors like the Einstein Telescope (ET). Although Pop III stars are thought to have been the progenitors of the very first stars and galaxy-seeding supermassive black holes, determining whether they left behind "stalled" surfaces remains uncertain. If such objects exist, they would produce a distinct GW signature at ET, allowing us to probe the physics of high-redshift, massive, Population II stars. Conversely, the detection of redskinned remnants would offer new constraints on early stellar formation histories. If no such objects are found, it may indicate that the initial massive stars were already "naked," potentially confirming that the population's metal content was so low that stellar rotation played a definitive role in their evolution.

Although physical layer security (PLS) research has extensively explored single-user, single-carrier systems, significant research gaps remain regarding PLS in multi-carrier (MC) wireless environments. Addressing this, this paper investigates a PLS-enhanced, AF-relay-assisted MC system where a trusted AP transmits $K$ orthogonal subcarriers through $N$ amplify-and-forward relays to $K$ single-carrier legitimate users, while simultaneously transmitting secure messages to illicit eavesdroppers. The study derives the secure capacity of this architecture and formulates an optimization problem aimed at maximizing this capacity by adjusting the AP's power distribution and relay gain parameters. The resulting problem is non-convex; however, the paper introduces a novel iterative algorithm that guarantees convergence to at least a stationary point solution. Key parameters influencing physical layer security are also analyzed. Finally, simulation outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed scheme, confirming its practical advantages.

Text-based interactive environments represent a robust framework for evaluating natural language understanding, common-sense reasoning, and virtual agent capabilities. We introduce \textbf{TextWorldExpress}, a high-performance Python implementation of the original TextWorld system that operates approximately 300 times faster, exceeding one million steps per second while preserving full API compatibility. We assert that this drastic increase in simulation throughput is crucial for conducting large-scale imitative learning experiments, a bottleneck that textworld's previous moderate processing speeds inherently limited. Empirical data demonstrates that our acceleration enables four standard reinforcement learning algorithms to generate policies capable of playing every scenario in the Environment more effectively than before. Furthermore, leveraging this boost in simulation speed, researchers deployed these algorithms in combination with research from prior studies—such as those addressing credit assignment, curricular learning, multi-tasking, and few-shot scenarios—resulting in agents that perform significantly better than those using just the base platform. We define this enhanced simulation velocity and throughput as "Expressiveness."

Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, despite their efficacy in video recognition tasks, consume excessive resources due to complex gate operations and redundant inter-neuron information, limiting widespread adoption. Consequently, this study introduces a hardware and method co-design approach targeting energy-efficient LSTMs via Tucker tensor decomposition. First, the authors propose the Cumulative-Update-Based Tucker Decomposition (CUTTC) algorithm, which addresses the non-cumulative limitation of existing iterative methods without requiring video re-replay. Second, the CUTTC framework integrates hardware-method co-design to achieve Hierarchical Tucker (HTTD) decomposition. This results in an 83.7% average data reduction for time-to-important features (TFs) compared to current techniques, yielding significant energy savings. Experimental data confirms that maintaining nearly 99.3% of the original model's accuracy, this method achieves a 90.6% decrease in system energy usage.

Rapid advancements in deep learning, particularly in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have enabled significant breakthroughs in image recognition. However, these models remain vulnerable to adversarial examples—subtly modified images that cause misclassification. This paper introduces "Interval ConvTuning," an efficient technique to enhance the robustness of CNNs by narrowing the bounds of values for activations. Experimental results demonstrate that applying Interval ConvTuning offers a strong combination of robustness and accuracy when tested on both natural and adversarial data. Furthermore, we establish a security argument for this integrity, proving that activation interval tuning inherently provides resistance to physical hardware faults. Our proof shows that with sufficiently tight bounds, the system remains invariant against specific single-bit flip (1-bit flip) faults affecting the weights of a proof's network. We propose a simple yet effective method to create multilingual word embeddings that preserve shared semantic structures across languages, driven by the hypothesis that items with identical representations in this space are linguistically related. Our approach initializes each language-specific embedding from that language's intrinsic structure, then progressively refines them so embeddings from different words map to identical points or adjacent regions within a cluster-tight semantic space. We evaluate these embeddings on standard cross-lingual tasks, including named entity recognition, machine translation, and vocabulary overlap, demonstrating significant improvements and notable gains over current state-of-the-art techniques. Our code and pre-trained embeddings are accessible via https://github.com/marco-tau/cluster2embeddings.

This study presents a detailed examination of pion, kaon, proton, antiproton, and $\phi$ meson production within the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) framework. All measured species are analyzed using standard thermal models, with proton and $\phi$ meson inclusions providing novel insights into these established applications. Results indicate that significant proton resonance contributions and strangeness equilibration occur approximately one femtometer per c ($1\,\text{fm}/c$) earlier than previously observed using only pions. Despite the incorporation of additional particle species, an excellent description of all yields is maintained using a single set of model parameters, highlighting the robustness of the canonical ensemble thermal approach. Furthermore, ratios normalized to pions—specifically $K/p$, $(p+\bar{p})/K$, and $Y/\pi$—are analyzed to offer new perspectives on the physical interpretation of particle abundance data.

In the latter half of October 2019, the capital of Chile, Santiago, experienced severe civil unrest that paralyzed the city for over a week. Drawing from a non-local epidemiological model featuring a short-term memory effect for the Santiago population, this study simulates the protest dynamics. The approach converts protest intensity into a pressure variable acting upon government policy; consequently, the intended transmission rate becomes a non-integrable function of this intensity. The results effectively replicate the epidemic curve observed in Chile and accurately reproduce key demographic details of the protest's intensity and duration. The methodology's success in reproducing these complex events highlights its potential for simulating similar historical or civil dynamics in the future.

This paper introduces a method to symbolically solve inequalities between extended regular languages, expressed as $r_1 \le r_2$. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on converting extended regular expressions into equivalent non-deterministic finite automata (NFAs)—a step often unfeasibly complex—the proposed algorithm constructs proof trees directly from the expression structure. The leaves of these trees yield sets of strings whose containment within specific sub-expressions is verified via simple checks, while internal nodes apply elementary inclusion tests. The final solutions emerge from combining these checks using the corresponding operational rules. The presented technique has already been implemented in the CREPE tool, designed to investigate connections between regular expression complexities and automated inference systems.

Visual-inertial navigation (VIN) for mobile units represents a well-established research domain, yet existing deep learning-based techniques often neglect the critical role of context, thereby hamming both training efficacy and navigation precision. Drawing an analogy to the human brain's utilization of long-term context, we introduce **External-Memory Visual-Inertial Navigation (EMA-VIO)**, a novel deep learning framework that integrates external memory mechanisms. Specifically, we develop an **External-Memory Visual-Inertial Network (EM-VIN)** to process external information and an attention module to integrate this information with current inertial and visual inputs, enabling it to adaptively concentrate on pertinent contextual elements. Furthermore, we outline a comprehensive framework combining EM-VIN networks, which delivers a direct solution for end-to-end mobile navigation tasks. Evaluation on both public datasets, collected in real-world urban environments, confirms that our proposed EM-VIN model significantly surpasses existing methods, with results from a heterogeneous robot platform further substantiating the approach's effectiveness.

Neutron star–black hole (NSBH) events produce distinctive gravitational-wave signatures that differ significantly from binary black hole (BBH) mergers. Training the DNN on a comprehensive dataset generated within this paper, it achieves an precision of 99.99% in identifying EM events associated with NSBH systems and maintains a recall of 99.99%. As higher masses for BH components increase, both the EM likelihood and the separability of NSBH signals improve; consequently, for the astrophysically relevant mass range where a BH is ten times heavier than a NS, the DNN maintains high accuracy with improved confidence. Given these capabilities, the DNN offers a swift method to flag candidate EM sources in observational data, enabling researchers to efficiently target and study NSBH events.

The regulation of friction is critical for controlling energy consumption and wear in mechanical systems. This study reveals that the friction coefficient of dry, liquid-alloy cell foams significantly decreases as surface roughness increases, a phenomenon driven by texture-induced stick-slip dynamics. While earlier research on soft, elastic materials like elastic dimers and spheres suggested that higher normal loads and interface roughness elevate friction by enhancing interlocking and contact points, our findings indicate the opposite for foam textures. Although elevated roughness raises local pressure peaks that promote plastic deformation and merge initially distinct textures, these conditions ultimately reduce friction. Contrasting with elastic solids, cell foams exhibit friction behavior governed by texture plasticity rather than elastic interactions.

The rapid advancement of deep learning has enabled these models to excel in various real-world applications, including medical diagnostics. Nevertheless, deploying these algorithms in clinical settings remains challenging, as models often struggle to generalize on unseen data, a phenomenon known as concept drift. This issue is frequently caused by imbalances between easy-in and hard-to-process samples. Although techniques like GANs and other entropy-based approaches have been developed to address difficult samples in medical contexts, existing entropy methods often fail to detect samples that are hard for a specific model. Consequently, this study introduces a novel entropy formulation and applies it to dermoscopic images for the task of skin cancer classification. The proposed method successfully identifies samples deemed challenging by a specific model, demonstrating an 8.5% overall boost in the five-class skin lesion classification benchmark using the ISIC 2019 dataset with a state-of-the-art state-of-the-art state-of-the-state model. The dataset and code are publicly available via https://github.com/ahmed-elsabagy/IDCDC2019.

This study examines the linear stability of a circular oil droplet within a Hele-Shaw cell subjected to rotation. When surface tension is neglected, the problem exhibits a singularly perturbed nature, where fingering instabilities arise when the spin rate drops below a critical threshold. Under slow rotational conditions, the system transforms into a non-autonomous ordinary differential equation. By applying perturbation methods and deriving a sideband evolution equation, we identify and characterize the feedback mechanisms between fingering patterns and the vorticity distribution. These approaches enable the construction of extended solutions that accurately model the complex, flexible finger structures observed in simulations.

The volatile organic compounds found in interstellar space, particularly those with carbon–carbon bonds, are currently the focus of significant study. While previous investigations have primarily tracked individual molecules or specific molecular classes separately, this work aims to determine the distribution of various CCH and CN derivatives associated with identified interstellar hydrocarbon rings. To achieve this, we utilize gas-phase chemical models alongside astronomical observations to identify potential targets for spectroscopic analysis within the dense molecular cloud TMC-1. Such structures were recently noted in TMC-1 via detections of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (HC≡C‑CPD) and cyclopentadiene (CPD). Our modeling results indicate that cyclopentadiene, ethynyl CPD, and these detected aromatics should exist at measurable levels in circumstellar regions, effectively ruling out their presence in interstellar grains or stellar outflows. Consequently, we focus our detection efforts on the dense molecular cloud TMC-1. We successfully identified two variants—dicyano cyclopentadiene (DCNCPD) and dicyno CCH cyclopentadiene (DCCNCPD)) within TMC-1, noting that DCNCPD is approximately 0.2 times more abundant than DCCNCPD relative to cyclopentadiene. These discoveries highlight a general trend where hydrocarbon rings in this environment preferentially bind CCH and CN groups.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) predominantly relies on context-aware attention mechanisms that adaptively determine the relevance of portions within a source text to generate specific words in the target text. While these mechanisms generally infer their scope retroactively, production scenarios demand real-time generation with limited or no buffering capacity, forcing attention to function prospectively. We introduce a novel, data-driven look-forward attention framework trained exclusively with monolingual parallelly translated datasets of similar linguistic characteristics through an end-to-end model training approach identified as "Synthetic Parallel Data (SPD)." This innovative design enables the model to detect where to project focus based on current output words, utilizing patterns inherent in bidirectional translation. Experiments conducted on three distinct languages demonstrate that these predicted attention mechanisms significantly enhance overall machine translation performance, validating the look-forward method's efficacy via improved outputs generated by the enhanced architecture.

Multivariate functional time series (MFTS) synchronously records the evolutionary trajectories of an extensive array of variables in continuous form over time. Despite the surging array of MFTS analytical techniques, few have specifically tackled Singular Functional Spectrum Analysis (SFA), a procedure widely adopted for scalar versions to streamline computations on temporal data by enhancing signal-to-noise ratios. Within this work, we present an adequate SFA framework tailored for MFTS that proceeds in two key stages: first, a smoothness-based basis is established for each dimension, allowing temporal patterns to be embedded directly without intermediate smoothing; subsequently, a split design is applied to construct smooth, trend-adjusted, and seasonal components of the data. Our contribution offers theoretical guarantees for asymptotic accuracy as either the time horizon or the variable count expands, while empirical results demonstrate its practical utility across both real-world applications and simulated tests.

Nuclei segmentation is a critical step in analyzing nucleus-based pathology, which aids significantly in diagnosing and treating diseases. Although existing methods have achieved strong performance, they often require a large amount of labeled data, intricate handcrafted features, and domain adaptation techniques to reach optimal results. Furthermore, the complexity of these approaches frequently hinders the efficient processing of large pathology datasets. Addressing these issues, this paper introduces a novel two-step nucleus identification framework based on a Dual-Stage Network (DSN). Initially, the network extracts salient nuclei regions from whole tissue samples; subsequently, shifted and resized whole-slide images (WSIs) are generated exclusively from those regions for further analysis. We evaluated this approach on three distinct datasets and found that the model effectively identifies nuclei within WSIs with high efficiency, requiring no labeled data, handcrafted features, or domain adaptation training. Specifically, in one experiment, the proposed method attained an Intersection over Union (IoU) score of 0.798 for segmenting all nuclei within a first step and accurately segmented all nuclei after re-evaluation in a second step achieving an IoU score of 0.888. The two-step network architecture demonstrated exceptional efficacy, particularly on the INPAH dataset where it reached an IoU score of 0.798 in the initial phase and 0.888 post-refinement.

Additionally, this approach elucidates why specific convolution operators exhibit superior performance on distinct graph structures. Establishing such a robust mathematical foundation holds significant promise for structuring innovative operator designs and guiding the creation of more effective GCNN architectures.

The capability to accurately determine vector boson fluxes formed by polarized muon beams stands as a critical requirement for designing experiments and analyzing data at High-Luminosity Muon Colliders. These flux calculations are typically complex, requiring extensive numerical integration and often taking considerable time to generate. However, existing efforts have already incorporated various strategies to enhance performance. In this study, we advance these efforts by applying the Randomized Neural Network (RNN) method specifically for predicting the angular distributions of vector bosons in High-Energy muon-muon collisions, focusing on key processes such as $\gamma$-exchange, $Z$-exchange, and their interference, as well as $W$-exchange and its interference with $\gamma$ and $Z$ exchange. Our findings reveal that for a sample of one million data points, the RNN approach achieves nearly identical results in both accuracy and computational speed compared to standard numerical integration methods when estimating the total exchanged charge squared fluxes; consequently, this neural network strategy is highly recommended for subsequent, more extensive calculations.

Multi-task reinforcement learning (MRL) aims to enhance an agent's generalization by sharing experiences across related tasks. A fundamental challenge in this domain is identifying the task connections that enable effective experience transfer. Recently, various methods have introduced external structures, such as hierarchical or modular relationships, to guide multi-task RL. This paper proposes a new approach that defines a modular structure based on the intrinsic similarities in the reward functions of those tasks. We provide theoretical proofs demonstrating that our method successfully prevents the destructive interference one task may cause to the learning of another within the system. Furthermore, through extensive experiments in both synthetic environments and a real-world robotic sub-rl setup, we show the superiority of our approach. These studies examine the number of tasks an agent can handle and evaluate the necessity of each dimension of the modular design, highlighting the importance of preventing destructive interference. Ultimately, our evidence supports the conclusion that careful prevention of interference is a critical component of building an efficient modular system.

Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (CGANs) represent a powerful Bayesian framework for computing full posterior distributions in inverse problems by employing empirical likelihood functions within the true prior. To resolve this, this study proposes a regularized conditional GAN that integrates a regularization term designed to enforce consistency with the true posterior mean squared. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis demonstrating that this formulation effectively mitigates issues in Bayesian machine learning caused by imprecise empirical likelihood functions. Finally, we validate our method through both controlled experiments and real-world applications.

The primary obstacle to utilizing pulsars for precise measurements of the interstellar plasma lies in the scattering and scintillation effects, which distort pulse profiles and spectra while inducing timing irregularities. Consequently, studying these phenomena is vital for understanding the interstellar medium (ISM) and accurately interpreting data from pulsars used for ISM measurements. In this work, we employed approximately 10,000 observations of pulsar PSR B1333+16, collected by the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR), to analyze scattering screens along its line of sight. The resulting dataset offers the most comprehensive scintillation observation of PSR B1333+16 to date. Our analysis reveals that the pulsar exhibits strong modulation in total power and, uniquely, distinct asymmetry in the scintillation spectra. Furthermore, detailed modeling of these spectra indicates the presence of multiple elongated scattering screens, or "filaments," oriented nearly parallel to the pulsar's velocity vector relative to the first dipole plane of the Galactic magnetic field. Such elongation is unexpected, as standard ISM theories suggest filamentation should result in perpendicular alignment. This discrepancy implies significant deviation from canonical interstellar models, potentially challenging current pulsar navigation algorithms. Therefore, investigations into pulsar scintillation and scattering are deemed essential.

We introduce Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), an autoregressive dilated convolutional neural network designed to generate realistic audio with controlled pitch. Addressing the limitation of standard WaveNet models, which require excessively large parameters for high-sample-rate audio, QPNet incorporates a novel "Dilated Residual Convolutional Pitch Embedding" to efficiently integrate pitch information. Additionally, we propose a "Dilated Convolutional Neural Network Gradient Pitch Estimator" capable of determining pitch directly from raw waveforms without relying on generative pitch-dependent gates. While these mechanisms support synthetic note playing, the model functions generally for any audio source. Acknowledging that current state-of-the-art WaveNet variants achieve the highest quality for unstructured synthesis, we establish a DNN baseline for generating free-text speech and music to demonstrate the inherent difficulty of synthesizing speech autonomously within our framework. Ultimately, we confirm the model's viability by successfully demonstrating the generation of multiple diverse audio types, including real-time, high-fidelity free-text speech music.

This paper examines canonical equilibrium conditions within Hilbert space using the Weyl-Wigner representation. It is demonstrated that the Liouville equation transforms into a hierarchy of infinite differential integral operator equations in phase space, whereas conditions for equilibrium take a much more compact form in this framework. Additionally, various two-level system scenarios are illustrated using the Weyl-Wigner method.

The concept of negative absolute temperature, though seemingly counterintuitive, has historically fascinated and challenged the minds of great physicists. For them, it was impossible not to engage with this topic, even if only to express their bewilderment. Unfortunately, much of the existing literature conveys such a strong sense of confusion regarding negative absolute temperatures that it may be difficult for current students to grasp the subject clearly. In contrast, this talk presents a non-confused perspective on why negative absolute temperatures matter and how they fit within statistical and thermal physics, offering an overview of relevant research and highlighting open questions for future investigation.

We analyze the phenomenology of an extended Higgs sector built upon the "basic scoto-seesaw" model. This framework incorporates a second light CP-even scalar and multiple new interaction terms, which generate complex structures in both the dark matter relic density and the scalar beta-function. By integrating two loops of radiative corrections into a comprehensive global fit of experimental and observational constraints, we explore the parameter space. Our findings indicate that stability of the Higgs potential in the vacuum allows a more extensive range of the chi-field, yet a specific subset of parameters remains consistent with current data while simultaneously satisfying phenomenological requirements for thermal WIMP dark matter within the new CP-even scalar sector.

Illness-aware image modification (IWM) serves as an effective strategy to protect the privacy of individuals in medical data sharing. Nevertheless, most existing approaches fail to incorporate disease knowledge, which can be gained from other clinical sources, potentially leading to suboptimal privacy protection. To address this, we introduce a framework named Illness-Knowledge Guided IWM (IKG-IWM). First, utilizing a disease recognition model, we generate an illness map for every patient that maps anatomical regions of abnormality on X-rays. Next, we construct an illness mask by segmentating these abnormal regions, which subsequently guides the injection of noise during the modification process. Our framework ensures that known pathological regions remain clear, while noise is added only to healthy regions of the image. This preservation of diagnostic integrity allows the method to be flexible with various disease-aware models. We validated our framework's efficacy through rigorous experiments on a public dataset, confirming not only strong reversibility and robustness but also minimal impact on diagnostic performance.

ViDaExpert serves as a specialized utility for rendering and analyzing multidimensional vector information, a resource crucial across disciplines ranging from biology to economics. This program enables vector data to appear interactively via two primary techniques: View Switching, which rapidly filters a dataset by specific variable values for detailed study, and VOPs (Volume Opposites Points), a technique rendering four-dimensional points—comprising a three-dimensional coordinates and an additional attribute—relative to a chosen reference point in that space. Uniquely, VODs allow for the clear, interactive presentation of four dimensions within what appears to be standard 3D context, facilitating immediate insights into complex, high-dimensional datasets.
